_comment: Phase 1: the five foundation levels, all on one engine.
Levels 6-40 are specified in docs/COLOR_SWEEPER_BUILD_PLAN.md and not built.
`params.level` is this skill's own ordering; the number a child sees is the
lesson's position in course.json, and the course test holds the two in step.

lessons.title: Touching Tiles
lessons.concept: Which Tiles Touch a Tile

play.targetObjective: Find every tile that touches the outlined one, including the four corner-touching ones.
stepByStep: Find the outlined tile.
Tap the tiles directly above, below, left and right of it.
Then tap the four that touch it only at a corner.
play.kidTip: A tile in the middle touches eight others. The corners count.
play.audioPrompt: Tap every tile that touches the outlined one. Do not forget the corners.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Every clue in this skill counts a neighbourhood, so a child who is unsure which tiles are in one cannot read a single clue correctly. This is built by tapping rather than told, because the corners are the part that gets forgotten.

lessons.title: Edges and Corners
lessons.concept: Neighbourhoods at the Side of a Board

play.targetObjective: Find every tile that touches an outlined tile sitting at the side or in a corner.
stepByStep: Find the outlined tile and notice it is at the side of the board.
Tap only the tiles that are really there.
A tile off the edge of the board does not exist, so it cannot touch anything.
play.kidTip: At a side there are five. In a corner there are only three.
play.audioPrompt: This one is at the side. Tap only the tiles that are really on the board.

lessons.pedagogyTip: A child who has only met the middle of a board learns 'eight' as the answer rather than as a count. An edge clue reading 5 then looks like a mistake in the puzzle.

lessons.title: Matching Colours
lessons.concept: Counting the Neighbours That Match

play.targetObjective: Count how many of the tiles touching the outlined one are the same colour as it.
stepByStep: Look at the outlined tile's own colour.
Check each tile around it, one at a time.
Count only the ones that match. The outlined tile is not one of them.
play.kidTip: Count the matching ones, not all of them.
play.audioPrompt: How many tiles touching this one are the same colour as it?

lessons.pedagogyTip: This is what a clue's number is, arrived at by counting before it is ever read off a tile. The count and the clue meet in the next lesson.

lessons.title: What a Clue Says
lessons.concept: Reading a Colour Clue

play.targetObjective: Say exactly what a clue claims: which colour it counts, and how many of the tiles it touches.
stepByStep: Read the colour of the tile the number is written on.
Read the number.
Say it as a sentence about the tiles it touches — not about itself.
play.kidTip: A clue never counts its own tile.
play.audioPrompt: What does this clue say? Read the colour as well as the number.

lessons.pedagogyTip: The board is blank apart from the clue on purpose. If the neighbours were coloured a child could answer by counting the picture and never read the clue at all, which is the thing this lesson exists to test.

lessons.title: The Other Colour
lessons.concept: What a Clue Says About the Colour It Does Not Name

play.targetObjective: Work out how many of a clue's neighbours are the other colour, from the clue and the size of its neighbourhood.
stepByStep: Count how many tiles the clue touches altogether.
The clue says how many of them are its own colour.
There are only two colours, so the rest are the other one.
play.kidTip: Every clue tells you two numbers, not one.
play.audioPrompt: This clue counts one colour. How many are the other one?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Unlike a mine, which is either there or not, every tile here has a colour — so an orange three also says five are navy. That second number is free, and it is what makes clues of different colours comparable later on.

lessons.title: Zero Means None
lessons.concept: A Zero Clue Rules a Colour Out

play.targetObjective: Use a zero clue to colour every tile it touches.
stepByStep: Find the clue with a 0 on it.
Nothing it touches can be that colour.
Colour every blank tile it touches the other colour.
play.kidTip: Zero means none of that colour, not none of any colour.
play.audioPrompt: This clue says zero. Colour the tiles it touches.

lessons.pedagogyTip: A zero is the only clue a child can act on without counting anything, which is why it comes first. The risk is reading it as ‘empty’ rather than as a count of one colour.

lessons.title: Zero at an Edge
lessons.concept: A Zero Clue in a Clipped Neighbourhood

play.targetObjective: Use a zero clue that sits at the side or corner of the board.
stepByStep: Find the zero and trace the tiles it really touches.
Tiles off the edge of the board do not exist.
Colour the blank ones the other colour.
play.kidTip: A corner clue touches only three tiles.
play.audioPrompt: This zero is in a corner. Which tiles does it actually touch?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Joins the neighbourhood work of level 2 to the deduction of level 6. A child who counts eight out of habit will colour a tile the clue never mentioned.

lessons.title: Every Neighbour Matches
lessons.concept: A Clue That Fills Its Whole Neighbourhood

play.targetObjective: Use a clue whose number equals the tiles it touches.
stepByStep: Count how many tiles the clue touches.
Compare that with the clue's number.
If they are the same, every one of them is that colour.
play.kidTip: When the number is as big as it can be, there is nothing left to decide.
play.audioPrompt: This clue counts every tile it touches. What colour are they?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The mirror of zero, and worth teaching straight after it: both are the cases where a clue decides its whole neighbourhood at once, so a child meets the shape of a deduction before meeting its arithmetic.

lessons.title: Matches Already Found
lessons.concept: A Clue Whose Count Is Already Met

play.targetObjective: Find a clue that already has all the matches it needs, and colour the rest.
stepByStep: Pick a clue and count the tiles round it that already match its colour.
Compare that with the clue's number.
If it already has enough, nothing else it touches can be that colour.
play.kidTip: A clue that has what it needs rules out everything else it touches.
play.audioPrompt: Count what this clue already has. Does it need any more?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The first lesson where a clue's number has to be compared with something rather than simply read. Zero and full needed no counting; this one does.

lessons.title: One More Match
lessons.concept: Deducing the Last Tile a Clue Needs

play.targetObjective: Work out the single tile a clue still needs.
stepByStep: Count the matches the clue already has.
Take that away from the clue's number.
If one is missing and only one tile is blank, that tile is the one.
play.kidTip: Clue number, minus what it already has, is what is left to find.
play.audioPrompt: This clue still needs one more. Which tile is it?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Subtraction inside a clue, with only one place for the answer to go. The arithmetic and the deduction are separated on purpose: level 11 keeps the arithmetic and takes away the single space.

lessons.title: All the Rest Match
lessons.concept: When the Spaces Left Equal the Matches Left

play.targetObjective: Fill every remaining tile when a clue needs exactly as many as are left.
stepByStep: Work out how many matches the clue still needs.
Count the blank tiles it touches.
If the two numbers are the same, every one of those tiles matches.
play.kidTip: Same number of spaces as matches still needed means they all match.
play.audioPrompt: How many does this clue still need, and how many spaces are left?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The same subtraction as level 10 with more than one tile to place, which is where a child stops guessing which one and starts reasoning about all of them. Corner clues are excluded on purpose: a corner touches three tiles, so a clue needing three of them is level 8's whole-neighbourhood rule wearing this lesson's name.

lessons.title: Follow the Clues
lessons.concept: Using a Tile You Just Worked Out

play.targetObjective: Solve a board where one deduction is only possible after another.
stepByStep: Find the one clue you can act on straight away.
Colour what it tells you.
Now look again: a clue that was stuck may not be any more.
play.kidTip: A tile you have just worked out is evidence for the next clue.
play.audioPrompt: Start with the clue you can already use, then look again.

lessons.pedagogyTip: The first board that cannot be finished in one move. Until here every deduction stood alone; this is where a child has to use their own answer as evidence.

lessons.title: Shared Neighbours
lessons.concept: Comparing Two Clues That Overlap

play.targetObjective: Use two overlapping clues to settle the tiles they can, and leave the rest blank.
stepByStep: Find two clues that touch some of the same tiles.
Separate the tiles they share from the tiles only one of them touches.
Take the smaller clue away from the bigger one. What is left over is decided.
Leave every other tile blank — these two clues cannot decide it yet.
play.kidTip: Two clues can settle some tiles and not others. Blank is a real answer here.
play.audioPrompt: These two clues share some tiles. Colour only what they can settle.

lessons.pedagogyTip: The plan's own point: a lesson that demanded a finished board here would be asking a child to guess the rest, and teaching that guessing is how you finish. Leaving a tile blank because no clue decides it is the answer, and level 14 completes the same board.

lessons.title: Finish the Board
lessons.concept: Completing a Board After a Reduction

play.targetObjective: Reduce two overlapping clues, then use what that tells you to finish the board.
stepByStep: Start with the reduction: subtract the smaller clue from the bigger one.
Colour the tiles it settles.
Now read the clues again — one of them can decide more than it could before.
Keep going until every tile has a reason.
play.kidTip: A tile you worked out by comparing clues is evidence for the next clue.
play.audioPrompt: Compare the two clues first, then use what you find to finish.

lessons.pedagogyTip: The same board as level 13, asked to the end. Splitting them is deliberate: a child who can reduce but cannot see what the reduction unlocks has learned a trick rather than a method.

lessons.title: The 1-2-1 Wall
lessons.concept: A Named Pattern, and the Rule Behind It

play.targetObjective: Solve a wall of clues reading 1-2-1 by subtracting, not by remembering.
stepByStep: Write down what each clue still needs.
The middle clue covers everything the outer ones do, and one tile more.
Subtract an outer clue from the middle one.
Some walls read 1-2-1 and do not come out the same way — read yours.
play.kidTip: The shape is a result. The subtraction is the reason.
play.audioPrompt: Three clues in a row. Work out what each one still needs.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Minesweeper guides teach 1-2-1 as a picture to memorise. A child who learns only the picture cannot solve a wall that does not contain one, so this lesson mixes in a wall that reads 1-2-1 and settles differently — the memorised answer is wrong there and the subtraction is right.

lessons.title: The 1-2-2-1 Wall
lessons.concept: The Same Subtraction, One Step Further

play.targetObjective: Carry the same reduction along a longer wall.
stepByStep: Start at one end and subtract, exactly as before.
That settles one tile.
Use it, then subtract at the other end.
Check every clue against what you have written.
play.kidTip: A longer wall is not a new rule. It is the same one, used twice.
play.audioPrompt: Four clues this time. Start at one end.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Proof that the rule generalises and the picture does not: a child holding only the 1-2-1 shape has nothing to apply here, while a child holding the subtraction simply does it twice.

lessons.title: Count the Other Colour
lessons.concept: Reading a Clue as the Colour It Does Not Name

play.targetObjective: Turn a clue into a statement about the other colour, so two clues counting different colours can be compared.
stepByStep: One clue counts orange. The other counts navy.
Count how many tiles the navy clue touches altogether.
Take its number away: the rest of those tiles are orange.
Now both clues talk about orange, and you can compare them.
Colour only what that settles.
play.kidTip: Two clues can only be compared once they count the same colour.
play.audioPrompt: One clue counts orange and one counts navy. Say them both in the same colour first.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Every tile here has a colour, unlike a mine, which is there or not. So a clue states two numbers and the second is free. This is where that free number starts doing work, and it is what makes clues of different colours comparable at all.

lessons.title: How Many Are Left
lessons.concept: A Count for the Whole Board

play.targetObjective: Use the strip above the board, which counts a colour across every tile.
stepByStep: Read the total at the top: that is for the whole board, not one clue.
Count how many of that colour are already there.
Take one from the other.
If none are left, every blank tile is the other colour.
play.kidTip: Count every tile on the board, not the ones near the blanks.
play.audioPrompt: The strip at the top counts the whole board. How many are already there?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The first clue that is not about a neighbourhood at all. A child who has only met clues sitting on tiles will look for one near the blanks and find nothing; the information is there, in a place they have not learned to look.

lessons.title: A Whole Row
lessons.concept: A Clue That Counts Along a Line

play.targetObjective: Use a clue that counts a colour along one row or column.
stepByStep: Read which row or column the clue names.
Trace that line with a finger, and nothing else.
Count the ones already that colour.
If the line has all it needs, the rest of it is the other colour.
play.kidTip: A line clue counts along its line. Tiles above and below do not count.
play.audioPrompt: This clue counts along one row. Which tiles are in it?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The neighbourhood habit is strong by now, and this is where it misleads: a child who counts the tiles around the clue instead of along the line gets a different number and no warning.

lessons.title: A Marked Area
lessons.concept: A Clue That Counts Inside an Outline

play.targetObjective: Use a clue that counts a colour inside a marked area of any shape.
stepByStep: Find the outlined tiles. The outline is part of the board.
Count only what is inside it.
Compare that with the clue's number.
A tile just outside the outline does not count, however close it is.
play.kidTip: Trace the outline first. Then count only what is inside it.
play.audioPrompt: The outlined tiles are the ones this clue counts.

lessons.pedagogyTip: The last step away from the neighbourhood: an area with no rule to its shape, so the only way to know what is counted is to look. The outline is drawn with the board rather than offered as a hint, because it is part of the puzzle.

lessons.title: All in a Run
lessons.concept: A Line Clue Whose Tiles Sit Together

play.targetObjective: Use a line clue that says its tiles sit side by side.
stepByStep: Read the clue: how many, and that they are together.
One tile in the line is already that colour, so the block includes it.
Work out where a block that size can sit and still cover it.
Everything outside the block is the other colour.
play.kidTip: The count says how many. Together says where they can be.
play.audioPrompt: These tiles sit side by side. Where can the block start?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The count on its own leaves several arrangements here, so a child who reads only the number cannot finish. That is deliberate: the condition has to change the answer, or the lesson is the previous one with different punctuation.

lessons.title: A Gap Somewhere
lessons.concept: A Line Clue Whose Tiles Do Not All Touch

play.targetObjective: Use a line clue that says its tiles are not all together.
stepByStep: Read the clue: how many, and that they do not all touch.
List the ways that many could sit in the line.
Cross out every arrangement where they are all side by side.
If one arrangement is left, that is the answer.
play.kidTip: Ruling an arrangement out is a move. It is how this clue works.
play.audioPrompt: These do not all touch. Which arrangement does that rule out?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The same count as the last lesson with the opposite condition, which is the cleanest way to show that the condition and not the number is doing the work. Rejecting a placement is the move, so the hint shows the rejected one rather than skipping to the answer.

lessons.title: Three Colour Choices
lessons.concept: Excluding One Colour Still Leaves Two

play.targetObjective: Work out a tile's colour when two clues each rule one colour out.
stepByStep: Start with all three colours as possibilities for the blank tile.
Read the first clue and cross out what it forbids.
Two are still left, so keep both.
Read the second clue and cross out again. One remains.
play.kidTip: Not orange does not mean navy when there are three colours.
play.audioPrompt: Three colours this time. One clue is not enough.

lessons.pedagogyTip: The habit built by every two-colour board is that ruling one colour out decides the tile. Here it does not, and a child who carries the habit over will answer confidently and wrongly.

lessons.title: Clues of Different Colours
lessons.concept: Comparing Clues That Count Different Colours

play.targetObjective: Use clues counting different colours together, and colour only what they settle.
stepByStep: Read what each clue counts — they are not all the same colour.
Over the same three tiles, work out how many of the third colour there must be.
Now compare the two clues that count that colour.
Only the tile they both cover is settled. Leave the others blank.
play.kidTip: Work out the colour nobody counted, then compare.
play.audioPrompt: These clues count different colours. Find the one nobody mentioned.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Three tiles, one cyan and one navy among them, so exactly one is orange: the counts over a set always add up to its size. That is the same free number level 5 introduced, doing the work here that the reduction alone cannot.

lessons.title: Three Colour Totals
lessons.concept: One Total for Each Colour

play.targetObjective: Use a separate board total for each colour, one colour at a time.
stepByStep: Take one colour and count how many of it are already on the board.
Compare that with its own total. If it is used up, no blank tile is that colour.
Do the same for the next colour.
A clue then separates the last two tiles.
play.kidTip: Each colour has its own total. Never add them together.
play.audioPrompt: Three totals, one for each colour. Take them one at a time.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Tametsi gives a total per colour rather than one number, and this is why: with three colours a single total says almost nothing, while three of them can finish a board no neighbourhood clue reaches.

lessons.title: Every Kind of Clue
lessons.concept: Choosing Which Clue Can Still Help

play.targetObjective: Finish a board that mixes several kinds of clue, choosing which to read next.
stepByStep: Look at every clue on the board, and notice they are not all the same kind.
Find one that can say something right now.
Colour what it settles.
When the clues around a tile run out, ask which other kind still reaches it.
play.kidTip: When you are stuck, change the kind of clue you are reading.
play.audioPrompt: This board mixes clue kinds. Which one can help first?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Every earlier lesson told a child which technique to use by being about it. This one does not, and choosing is the skill: a board with a total, a line, a region and a neighbourhood on it is stuck only until you look somewhere else.

lessons.title: Which Clues Help
lessons.concept: Judging Whether Evidence Is Enough

play.targetObjective: Decide which clues are enough, on their own, to settle a tile.
stepByStep: Look at the outlined tile.
Take one set of clues and imagine the others were not there.
Ask whether the tile still comes out.
A clue can be true and still say nothing about this tile.
play.kidTip: True is not the same as useful. Ask what each clue decides.
play.audioPrompt: Which of these clues would be enough on their own?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Making a deduction and knowing what it rested on are different skills, and only the second survives a board a child has not seen. Every option here is re-solved when it is chosen, so a set nobody expected is accepted if it works.

lessons.title: Explain the Move
lessons.concept: Saying Why a Move Works

play.targetObjective: Choose a statement that really explains why a tile must be its colour.
stepByStep: Read what the move claims.
A reason has to name a clue.
It has to say what that clue counts, and where.
Then it has to say what that leaves for this tile.
play.kidTip: More than one of these can be a fair way of saying it.
play.audioPrompt: Which of these says why the tile must be that colour?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Two of the options are the same reason worded differently and both are accepted, because a child who says it their own way has not made a different move. What separates the wrong ones is what they claim a clue counts.

lessons.title: Spot a Contradiction
lessons.concept: Finding the Clue a Board Breaks

play.targetObjective: Find a clue that the coloured board does not satisfy.
stepByStep: Pick a clue and read its colour and number.
Count that colour around it.
If the two disagree, that clue is broken.
If they agree, move to the next clue.
play.kidTip: One wrong tile can break more than one clue. Any of them is a right answer.
play.audioPrompt: One tile here is wrong. Which clue is no longer true?

lessons.pedagogyTip: Checking is not solving backwards: a child is given a finished board and has to test it, which is the first time in this skill that being able to say a thing is wrong matters more than being able to get it right.

lessons.title: Check a Three-Colour Board
lessons.concept: Auditing Somebody Else's Three-Colour Work

play.targetObjective: Audit a three-colour board and find the clue it breaks.
stepByStep: Read the clue's colour first — with three in play it matters more.
Count only that colour around it.
Compare with the number.
A tile of the third colour is neither right nor wrong until you check the clue that counts it.
play.kidTip: Count the clue's own colour. Ignore the other two.
play.audioPrompt: Three colours, and one tile is wrong. Which clue does it break?

lessons.pedagogyTip: The counting error this catches is specific to three colours: a child who counts 'tiles that are not the clue's colour' gets a number that is right for two colours and wrong here.

stepByStep: Read the board.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Labelled with the foundation key it reviews, not with all four it exercises: an aggregate score across four techniques is not evidence of any one of them.

lessons.pedagogyTip: One technique, nine times, at every board position it can take.

play.targetObjective: Answer nine on your own, with no hints and nothing read aloud.

lessons.pedagogyTip: The corner case matters most here: a corner clue needing three is the whole neighbourhood, and a child who has only seen centres will not expect it.

lessons.pedagogyTip: Three subtraction boards to one chain, because the chain is the same subtraction used twice and the arithmetic is what needs the repetitions.
